extracted.intended_audience: journalists, news editors, media researchers, and students of international news and media policy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and hypotheses about what makes events from other countries enter the news and how such selection shapes images of foreign nations; intended to guide analysis of foreign news selection and suggestions for newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: (4,3) The more distant an event, the less ambiguous will it have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: For remote events to make news they must be simple; complexities can be handled when they occur within one's own culture but not at a considerable distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culturally distant events are presented as 'ideal types' and described in sweeping, uniform terms; this simplification fosters impressions of uniformity and of those countries as inherently different or dangerous. News from distant places must therefore avoid ambiguity and complexity to pass selection filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: (4,5) The more distant the nation, the more consonant will the news have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: Far-away nations make news most readily when the story fits pre-existing patterns or expectations (is 'consonant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military coups in Latin America are reported because they fit expectations; developments inconsistent with stereotypes are less reported or dismissed as fake. Stories consonant with 'mental pre-image' pass many filters; non-consonant positive or atypical items are often ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: (7,2) The higher the continuity effect, the lower can the threshold be
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an event has entered the news channel, follow-up events encounter a lower threshold for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates 'news strings' and can produce artificial continuities simply because the channel is already open. Follow-ups are more easily reported even if individually they would not meet usual thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: (8,2) The higher the composition effect, the lower can the threshold be
rubrics_metrics.description: News items may be selected to correct under-representation of categories, lowering the threshold for what counts as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In quiet periods, editors may include low-scoring items to fill category quotas, producing images of discontinuity that don't match reality. This selection logic is part of the composition effect—coverage chosen for representational balance rather than intrinsic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: (1,12) The less negative the news, the more important the frequency condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive events need to be particularly short-lived or concentrated to register as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a premium on ceremonies or staged events where long-term developments are telescoped into a reportable moment; adding elite participants increases newsworthiness. This skews reporting toward visible, elite-managed positive events and encourages PR activity while downplaying sustained, non-ceremonial work by non-elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,4) The lower the rank of the nation, the lower must the cultural distance be
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-ranked nations must be more proximate (culturally/geographically) to receive coverage comparable to higher-ranked nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top nations have networks of 'underlings' they over-report from (e.g., U.S.—Latin America). This pattern reinforces world divisions and fosters identification-based reporting biased toward certain relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,5) The lower the rank of the nation, the more consonant will the news have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: News from low-ranked countries must fit stereotypes or expected narratives to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical coverage emphasizes difficulties (payment crises, political instability, elite murders), reinforcing images of immaturity or incapacity. This mirrors the distance–consonance hypothesis but specifically tied to perceived international rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: (:10,6) The lower the rank of the person, the more unexpected will the news have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary (low-rank) people only make news when something highly contrasting or unexpected happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elite routines are reported regularly; rank-and-file people enter the news primarily via dramatic contrasts such as sudden wealth or extreme negative acts. Routine positive or ordinary actions by common people rarely meet news thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,10) The lower the rank of the nation, the higher will a person have to be placed in that nation to make news
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals from low-ranked nations must be high-status (elite) to be newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to images of underdog nations as elite-dominated and underrepresents the mass population, making identification by readers difficult and reinforcing elite-focused narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: The lower the rank of the nation, the more negative will the news from that nation have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of underdog nations tends to be overwhelmingly negative; positive developments are under-reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include frequent disaster or coup coverage from such countries. The bias produces images of incapacity and inferiority relative to 'topdog' nations, because positive events in low-ranked countries often fail to pass news filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: (10,12) The lower the rank of a person, the more negative will his actions have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: Common people must perform negative acts to enter news; positive acts by ordinary people are less likely to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While sport, arts and entertainment can counterbalance this, most positive, everyday actions fail to satisfy criteria of frequency, threshold, unexpectedness and continuity. Ordinary people's positive roles typically appear only in feature or article-reportage forms rather than routine news.

rubrics_metrics.name: (11,12) The less personal the news, the more negative will it have to be
rubrics_metrics.description: Events not attributed to persons (natural or impersonal causes) must be negative to qualify as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects a dominant narrative that depicts humans as agents of progress while non-personal forces (floods, earthquakes) are newsworthy primarily when negative; impersonal positive developments are less likely to be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined effect: cultural distance + low international rank
rubrics_metrics.description: When cultural distance and low international rank are superimposed, news from such countries must refer to people (preferably elite), be negative, unexpected, consonant with pre-existing images, simple, and provide identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such coverage tends to portray peripheral countries as dangerous, elite-ruled, unchanging, and existing for the benefit (or detriment) of center nations; events are sudden, fit stereotypes, and lack build-up or follow-up in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 1: Emphasize build-up and background material
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase emphasis on background and long-term development in media output; train journalists to capture and report long-term processes rather than focusing on isolated events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reduce event-centric reporting which overstates suddenness and unpredictability in foreign contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 2: Report occasional trivial items
rubrics_metrics.description: Include occasional reports on trivial matters even if they do not 'make news' to counterbalance a world-image composed of dramatic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing some non-event items helps reduce the distortion of reality into strings of dramatic occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 3: Emphasize complex and ambiguous events
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more coverage to complex, ambiguous events without necessarily forcing interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should encourage handling ambiguity rather than simplifying foreign events into easy narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 4: Report more from culturally distant zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase reporting from culturally distant areas even when immediate relevance is low; experiment with cross-country local column exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This counters over-reliance on culturally proximate stories and broadens perspectives beyond historically reprinted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 5: Emphasize dissonant information and challenge stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus more on information that does not fit stereotypes; train journalists to recognize and counteract their own stereotypes and the consonance factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active awareness-raising and training can reduce automatic acceptance of consonant stories and improve coverage diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 6: Emphasize predictable and frequent events
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more emphasis to predictable, frequent phenomena for balance, as a counterweight to event-driven drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular coverage of everyday or frequent occurrences helps correct skewed impressions created by selective dramatic reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 7: Increase awareness of continuity and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of the continuity effect and prioritize follow-up reporting even after interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report not only negative incidents but how they are addressed over time, preventing one-off negative stories from being the lasting impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 8: Be aware of the composition effect to avoid news artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize how attempts to fill representational categories can create artefactual 'news'; adjust selection to avoid misleading discontinuities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should distinguish genuine newsworthiness from coverage chosen solely to balance categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 9: More coverage of non-elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase coverage of nations not in the elite/topdog category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader geographic balance reduces center-periphery distortions in international news images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 10: More coverage of non-elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: Include more stories about ordinary people rather than focusing almost exclusively on elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves identification and counters elite-dominated portrayals of foreign societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 11: More reference to non-personal causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase attention to impersonal, structural or systemic causes of events rather than attributing everything to individual actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special training is recommended to identify and report non-personal causal factors effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication 12: More reference to positive events
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately report more positive developments from foreign nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counteracts pervasive negativism in foreign news and helps present a more balanced image of other countries.
